title: Does the Erdős–Purdy property hold with n−4 obstacles? (Erdős #105 OQ-01)
problemStatement: For all n ≥ 5, do n non-collinear points A in the plane together with n−4 disjoint obstacle points B always admit a line through ≥ 2 points of A that avoids all of B? Equivalently, is the threshold f(n) = n−4 (its maximum possible value given Xichuan's 2024 disproof of the n−3 case)? OPEN.

insights: The Erdős–Purdy obstacle-avoidance property is antitone in the number of obstacles: surviving m+1 obstacles implies surviving m. Proof is a padding argument — place one extra obstacle in the infinite plane outside A ∪ B, solve the harder instance, and the rich line returned avoids the original smaller obstacle set.
The only non-formal ingredient in the reduction is that ℝ² is infinite, so a finite point/obstacle configuration always leaves room for one more obstacle.

Monotonicity locates OQ-01 exactly: a positive answer forces survival at every obstacle count m ≤ n−4, pinning f(n)=n−4 against Xichuan's n−3 failure; a negative answer (an n−4 counterexample) would manufacture a fresh n−3 counterexample, strictly stronger than Xichuan's disproof.
OQ-01 is the genuine frontier: combined with f(n) ≤ n−4 (Xichuan) and f(n) ≥ cn (Beck/Szemerédi–Trotter), a YES is equivalent to f(n) = n−4 exactly.

knowledge.progressSummary: SURVEYED + INFRASTRUCTURE: created verified, axiom-free monotonicity reduction (0 axioms, 0 sorries) locating the open n−4 question exactly relative to Xichuan's n−3 disproof. The underlying yes/no question remains OPEN.

knownResults: Erdős–Purdy (1995): conjectured the n−3 version holds.
Beck / Szemerédi–Trotter (1983): with cn obstacles a rich unblocked line always exists, so f(n) ≥ cn.
Xichuan (2024): disproved the n−3 conjecture with three explicit counterexamples, so f(n) ≤ n−4. ($50 prize awarded.)
